common_name: Goliath Forage Rape (High-Yield Multi-Graze Brassica Cover Crop)

planting.note: Drill into a firm, moist seedbed in late summer for a leafy fall-to-winter grazing or biomass cover.

directions: Broadcast or drill shallowly into a well-prepared seedbed, since fine brassica seed only needs a light covering to establish. Goliath is a modern leafy forage rape bred for heavy total dry-matter output and good regrowth after a first grazing or mowing, holding its leaf quality into cooler weather better than older rape types. It pairs well with a cereal or ryegrass companion to spread grazing risk and add root structure to the stand. Terminate or graze down before bolting the following spring if left past one winter.

common_name: Titan Forage Rape (Fast-Establishing Summer and Fall Grazing Brassica)

planting.note: Sow from late spring through midsummer for a single-season grazing or green-manure brassica; also works as a late-summer sowing for fall feed.

directions: Drill or broadcast into a firm, fine seedbed, keeping the surface evenly moist until seedlings are established since brassica seed is small and shallow-sown. Titan is a quick-maturing forage rape prized for reaching grazable size faster than many kale-type brassicas, making it a flexible fit between two cash crops or as a catch crop after an early vegetable harvest. It tolerates one or two grazings or mowings with reasonable regrowth before quality declines. Rotate out of brassica-heavy fields to limit clubroot and other soilborne disease buildup.

common_name: Corsa Forage Kale (Giant-Type High-Biomass Cover Crop Kale)

planting.note: Sow in late spring to early summer for a tall standing crop stockpiled for late-fall and winter grazing or cutting.

directions: Direct sow in rows or broadcast at a wider spacing than turnip-type brassicas, since Corsa grows into a tall, thick-stemmed giant kale rather than a compact leafy mat. It is grown as a stockpiled standing forage, accumulating a large volume of dry matter through summer and fall that is then grazed, strip-grazed, or cut through the winter months. Its stature and cold tolerance make it one of the highest-yielding single-season brassica options where a long growing window is available. Allow extra time to full size compared with faster leafy turnip-rape hybrids before the first grazing or harvest.

common_name: Emblaze Forage Kale (Fast-Establishing High-Yield Cover Crop Kale)

planting.note: Sow in late spring for a fast-bulking kale stand grazed or cut from late summer through winter.

directions: Broadcast or drill into a firm, weed-free seedbed in late spring to early summer; Emblaze establishes and bulks up quickly relative to older giant kale types, shortening the wait before the first grazing. It holds leaf quality well into cold weather, continuing to provide green feed or biomass after frosts that would knock back less hardy cover crops. Strip-graze or mow in sections to limit trampling waste on the standing crop. Rotate with a non-brassica cover the following season to manage disease pressure.

common_name: Green Globe Forage Turnip (Multi-Purpose Bulb Cover Crop Turnip)

planting.note: Sow in summer to early autumn for a globe-rooted turnip grazed or lifted through fall and winter.

directions: Broadcast or drill shallowly into a firm, fine seedbed from midsummer through early fall, since this bulb turnip matures later than fast leafy types and is sown for winter rather than quick summer feed. Green Globe produces a large round root along with usable top growth, giving a dual-purpose cover that can be grazed for leaf first and then the root itself later in the season. It stores reasonably well in the ground under mild winter conditions, extending the grazing or harvest window. Rotate away from brassica-family crops the following year to reduce disease carryover.

common_name: Pallaton Raphno (Kale-Radish Interspecific Multi-Graze Forage Hybrid)

planting.note: Sow from late spring through late summer; this hybrid tolerates repeated grazing at almost any growth stage rather than needing one fixed maturity window.

directions: Drill into a firm, moist seedbed; this is a deliberate interspecific cross between forage kale and forage radish bred to combine the radish parent's deep taproot and drought tolerance with the kale parent's leafy, repeat-grazing habit. Unlike single-maturity brassica covers, it can be grazed, mowed, or rested and grazed again across most of the season, and it regrows from the crown after cutting rather than bolting to seed quickly. Its deep root also helps break up compacted layers while the top growth suppresses weeds. Because it is a complex hybrid, replanting from saved seed will not reliably reproduce the parent type.
